p1.title: Passage 1
paras: Homeopathy, a system of medicine developed in the 18th century, has gained increasing popularity in India as an alternative to conventional treatments. Based on the principle of “like cures like,” it employs highly diluted substances to stimulate the body’s natural healing mechanisms. Advocates claim efficacy in chronic conditions, minor ailments, and as complementary therapy alongside allopathy. Despite widespread use, homeopathy faces criticism due to a lack of empirical evidence, challenges in standardization, and debates over placebo effects. Regulatory frameworks in India aim to ensure quality control, professional training, and integration with national health programs. Patient preference, cultural acceptance, and affordability contribute to its continued growth. Emerging research explores homeopathy’s potential mechanisms, safety profiles, and role in holistic health, suggesting that its future hinges on reconciling traditional practice with scientific scrutiny.

p2.title: Passage 2
paras: The traditional linear economic model—predicated on an extractive "take-make-waste" philosophy—has driven global ecosystems to the brink of a waste crisis, choked by plastic pollution and hazardous electronic waste. For decades, municipal waste management relied on a "downstream" approach, focusing on expanding landfills and building energy-intensive incinerators. These methods merely conceal or transform garbage rather than eliminating its volume, releasing toxic leachates and greenhouse gases back into the environment. Transitioning to a circular economy requires an absolute "upstream" transformation, where products are intentionally engineered from inception for durability, modular disassembly, and complete material recovery. This shift demands strict Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) regulations that legally bind corporations to internalize the end-of-life environmental costs of their goods. Furthermore, upgrading the waste sector requires formalizing and protecting the informal recycling networks that handle waste collection in developing countries. Ultimately, a circular economy is not a simple community recycling initiative; it requires a complete decoupling of industrial economic growth from finite resource consumption.
